name: Infrastructure as Code
intent: Describe servers, networks and databases in versioned files, and let a tool compute and apply the difference between what the files say and what really exists.
scenario: A small stack: one network, two app servers and a database, written as declarative files in git. A pull request makes the servers bigger, someone resizes one by hand in the console, a database engine upgrade turns out to need a replacement, and a rename quietly destroys a server.
problem: Infrastructure built by clicking in a console cannot be reviewed, repeated or rolled back. Nobody knows exactly what exists or why, a second environment is a manual copy that slowly diverges, and a change made at 2 a.m. leaves no record. Rebuilding after a disaster means remembering clicks.

howItWorks.title: Declare the desired state in files
howItWorks.text: You write what should exist (a network, two servers of a given size and image, a database) in files kept in git. The files say what, not how. Resources can reference each other, so the tool knows the network must exist before the servers.

howItWorks.title: Plan: diff desired against real
howItWorks.text: The tool reads the code, refreshes its picture of the real world from the provider API, and compares the two. The result is a plan: resources to create, update in place, replace (destroy then create) or destroy. A plan changes nothing, so it can be attached to a pull request and reviewed like code.

howItWorks.title: Apply: execute exactly that plan
howItWorks.text: Apply performs the plan in dependency order: dependencies are created first and destroyed last. It is idempotent: the target is a state, not a list of commands, so running it again with nothing changed produces an empty plan and makes zero API calls.

howItWorks.title: State file and locking
howItWorks.text: The tool records which real resource (id) belongs to which block of code in a state file. Without it, it could not tell a renamed resource from a new one. The state lives in shared remote storage, and a lock stops two people applying at once and corrupting it. Treat state as sensitive: it often contains secret values.

howItWorks.title: Immutable attributes mean replace, not patch
howItWorks.text: Some attributes cannot be changed on a live resource (a database engine, a VPC address range, a server image). The plan marks these as forces replacement: the old resource is destroyed and a new one created. This is the immutable infrastructure idea, and it is also where data and uptime are lost if nobody reads the plan.

howItWorks.title: Detect and repair drift
howItWorks.text: If someone changes a resource by hand, real state no longer matches the code. The next plan notices (it refreshes first) and proposes reverting the change, or you update the code to adopt it. Drift detection can run on a schedule so surprises are found before an incident.

pros: Changes are reviewed, versioned and attributable like any code change
A plan shows the exact blast radius before anything is touched
Environments are repeatable: staging and production come from the same files
Disaster recovery and new regions become a re-apply instead of a memory test
Drift is detectable instead of invisible
cons: The state file is a new critical asset to store, back up, lock and protect
Plans can be large and hard to read, so reviewers skim and approve
Some changes destroy and recreate resources, and the tool will do it if you approve
Learning curve and tooling lock-in (provider quirks, state formats, language choice)
Console changes in an emergency still happen and then need reconciling
whenToUse: Anything you would otherwise need to build twice (staging and production, several regions or customers)
Teams where more than one person changes infrastructure and changes need review
Resources whose loss would hurt: networks, databases, IAM, DNS, where an audit trail matters
whenNotToUse: A throwaway prototype or a single personal server you will delete next week
Fast-changing data that is not configuration, such as rows in a table or objects in a bucket
Per-request or per-second scaling decisions: let an autoscaler change the count and have the code only set the bounds
pitfalls: Approving a plan without reading it: a one-word edit that says forces replacement on the production database is a data-loss event
Renaming a resource in code without a move or import step, which the tool reads as destroy the old one and create a new one
Secrets written into the code or the plan output; use a secrets manager and reference it, and remember the state file may still contain the value
One giant state for everything, so a mistake or a lock affects the whole company; split by environment and by service to limit blast radius
Hand edits in the console that never reach the code, so the next apply silently reverts an emergency fix
No deletion protection or backups on stateful resources, so a replace or destroy cannot be undone
Copy-pasted stacks instead of modules, which drift apart just like manual builds

roles.label: Config in git
roles.description: Declarative files describing the desired resources. Reviewed through pull requests.

roles.label: IaC tool
roles.description: Computes the plan by diffing desired against real, then applies it in dependency order.

roles.label: State file
roles.description: Remote, locked record of which real resource belongs to which block of code.

roles.label: Cloud provider
roles.description: The real servers, networks and databases. Also where hand edits happen.

quiz.question: A pull request changes the engine version of a production database in your declarative code. The plan shows the database with the note forces replacement, meaning destroy then create. What is the best action?
options: Apply it in a quiet window, since the tool creates the new database before removing the old one and keeps the data
Apply it and restore from the nightly backup afterwards, as replacements are a normal part of the workflow
Do not apply yet: replacement deletes the data, so plan an in-place upgrade or a migration with a backup
Delete the database from the state file so the tool no longer sees the change
quiz.explanation: A forced replacement destroys the old resource, and its data goes with it unless you plan for that. Removing it from state does not change the real database, it just leaves the tool blind to it.

quiz.question: During an incident someone enlarges an app server by hand in the cloud console. The code still says the smaller size. What does the next plan propose, and what is the right response if the larger size is wanted?
options: It sees no difference because the console edit is outside the tool's view, so nothing needs to be done
It proposes shrinking the server back to the coded size, so adopt the larger size in code via a pull request
It rewrites the code file to the larger size automatically, so the change is recorded without review
It fails with a lock error until someone removes the manually changed server from the state file entirely
quiz.explanation: The plan refreshes the real state first and treats the hand edit as drift to revert. If the change should stay, it belongs in code, reviewed like any other.

quiz.question: A server holds data on its local disk. An engineer renames its resource block in the code from web to app. The plan says 1 to destroy and 1 to create. Why, and what should be done?
options: The tool matches resources by their properties, so it saw a real change; accept the plan and apply it anyway
Names are only labels in the code, so the plan is wrong and should be re-run until it is empty
The state file is corrupted by the rename; restore an older state backup and apply the code again
The state maps the old name to the real server, so a rename looks new; add a move or state rename step
quiz.explanation: The state ties each real resource id to a block name, so a bare rename looks like removing one and adding another. A move or import step tells the tool it is the same server and avoids losing the disk.
